questions.stem: 'Submit your permission form to the office by Friday.' The verb form used here shows the writer is:
options: using high modality adjectives, which position the writer as uncertain about the request
using first person pronouns, which position the writer as an equal member of the group
using the imperative mood, which positions the writer as having authority to direct the reader
using the interrogative mood, which positions the writer as seeking information from the reader
questions.explanation: An imperative begins with a bare verb ('Submit') and directly commands the reader, so it constructs an unequal role: one person instructs, the other complies. The interrogative option is tempting because both imperatives and questions are directed at a reader, but interrogatives ask ('Have you submitted your form?') rather than direct. The cue is the missing subject before the verb — a sentence that starts with a plain verb and gives an instruction is imperative.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the HIGHEST modality?
options: Students must wear the school hat during all outdoor lessons.
Students should probably wear the school hat during outdoor lessons.
Students might like to wear the school hat during outdoor lessons.
Students could consider wearing the school hat during outdoor lessons.
questions.explanation: Modality is the degree of certainty or obligation in a statement; 'must' expresses the strongest obligation and leaves the reader no choice, which positions the writer as an authority. 'Should probably' is the most tempting alternative because 'should' does carry obligation, but 'probably' weakens it into advice. Rank modals as a ladder — must and will at the top, should and ought in the middle, might and could at the bottom.

questions.stem: A student emails a teacher about a late assignment. Which sentence best maintains a respectful, formal relationship?
options: Gonna be late with the essay, so Monday works better for me, thanks.
I was wondering whether it might be possible to submit my essay on Monday.
Just letting you know I'll be handing my essay in on Monday instead.
You need to give me until Monday because I couldn't finish the essay.
questions.explanation: Tentative modality ('might be possible') and an indirect question construct the teacher as the decision-maker, which suits an unequal, formal relationship. 'Just letting you know I'll be handing my essay in on Monday' is the most tempting distractor because it is polite in tone, but 'letting you know' announces a decision already made and removes the teacher's authority. Check who is given the power to decide — a request leaves it with the reader, an announcement takes it away.

questions.stem: Compare: (i) 'The Year 8 coordinator has cancelled the excursion.' (ii) 'The cancellation of the excursion has been confirmed.' The nominalised version (ii) changes the relationship with the reader by:
options: adding high modality, so readers understand the decision could still be reversed
turning a statement into a command, so readers know they must accept the decision
removing the person responsible, so the decision seems official rather than made by someone
making the writing more emotional, so readers feel the writer shares their disappointment
questions.explanation: Nominalisation turns the verb 'cancelled' into the noun 'cancellation', which lets the writer drop the agent; the event is then presented as an impersonal fact rather than a choice someone made. The 'more emotional' option is tempting because students associate rewriting with tone changes, but nominalisation does the opposite — it makes writing more abstract and distant. The cue is a noun where you expect a verb, plus a missing 'who did it'.

questions.stem: In a job interview, an applicant says: 'Certainly, Ms Patel — I'd be glad to explain how I handled that.' The vocative 'Ms Patel' mainly functions to:
options: shift the sentence into reported speech by naming the person addressed
acknowledge the interviewer's status and signal a courteous, formal relationship
identify the grammatical subject of the sentence so the meaning stays clear
raise the modality of the response so the claim sounds more certain
questions.explanation: A vocative is a name or title used to address someone directly; choosing the title plus surname rather than a first name marks respect and keeps the relationship formal and unequal in the interviewer's favour. The modality option is tempting because 'Certainly' in the same sentence does raise modality, but that work is done by the adverb, not by the name. A vocative can be removed without changing who does what in the sentence — that is the test.

questions.stem: In a school newsletter, the principal writes: 'We all need to look after our new library.' The pronoun 'we' mainly works to:
options: include the reader in a shared group, so the request feels like a joint responsibility
signal that the principal speaks only for staff, excluding students from the request
raise the modality of 'need', turning the sentence into a legal obligation
mark the sentence as passive voice, hiding who is responsible for the library
questions.explanation: Inclusive pronouns such as 'we' and 'our' place writer and reader inside the same group, which reduces the distance between them and reframes an instruction as a shared duty. The option about excluding students reverses this: 'we all' plus 'our new library' explicitly gathers everyone in, which is the opposite of exclusive use. A useful cue is to ask 'does this we include me, the reader?' — if yes, the writer is building closeness rather than issuing an order from above.

questions.stem: A school rule is being drafted. Which sentence positions the writer as distant and impersonal by removing the person who performs the action?
options: Phones will be confiscated if they are used during class time.
I will take your phone if I see you using it in class.
Ms Nguyen collects phones from students at the start of lessons.
Could you please keep your phone in your bag during class?
questions.explanation: Agentless passive voice ('will be confiscated') deletes the doer, so the rule seems to come from the institution rather than a named person, creating distance and authority. The version naming Ms Nguyen is tempting because it also sounds official, but it is active voice with the agent stated, so the responsible person is visible. Check who is doing the verb: if the sentence never says, it is agentless passive.

questions.stem: A manager says to a new employee: 'I was wondering if you might be able to finish the stocktake before you go today?' The language choices here mainly:
options: position the employee as higher in status by nominalising the verb 'take stock'
soften a directive through hedging and question form, while still expecting it to be done
remove the manager's authority so the task is genuinely optional for the employee
use high modality in 'might' and 'wondering' to fix a non-negotiable deadline
questions.explanation: Hedges such as 'I was wondering' and the low-modality 'might', combined with an interrogative structure, disguise an instruction as an enquiry, which protects the working relationship while the expectation of compliance remains. The claim that the task becomes genuinely optional is the closest trap: politeness markers change tone, not the underlying power relationship, and refusing would still carry consequences. Ask who has the authority in the situation — if the speaker outranks the listener, softeners are managing the relationship, not surrendering control.

questions.stem: Which sentence evaluates a novel using a metaphor?
options: The novel ends on page 312 with a short epilogue.
The novel's ending is a slammed door in the reader's face.
The novel's ending is as sudden as a slammed door.
The novel's ending is abrupt and left me unsatisfied.
questions.explanation: A metaphor states that one thing is another without a comparing word, and here the ending is said to be a slammed door, which carries the judgement that it shuts the reader out. The sentence using 'as sudden as' is tempting, but the signal word 'as' makes it a simile rather than a metaphor. The third option evaluates the ending but does so literally, with no figurative image at all.
questions.teaching:
Evaluating a text means judging it, and writers often reach for figurative language to make a judgement vivid.

A metaphor asserts the comparison outright rather than flagging it: it says the thing *is* something else, with no 'like' or 'as' to signal it. A simile keeps that linking word. So when sorting options, look for whether the comparison is signalled or simply stated. A sentence that describes the text plainly, without comparing it to anything, is not figurative at all — however strong its opinion.

questions.stem: In a review, the 'language of evaluation' refers to wording that:
options: expresses a judgement about the quality or worth of something
supplies factual evidence to back up a judgement already made
sets out events in the order in which they happened
tells the reader the steps needed to complete a task
questions.explanation: Evaluation is the language of judgement — words and images that tell the reader how good, bad, effective or disappointing something is. The option about supplying factual evidence describes substantiation, which supports evaluation but is not the same thing. Remember the pair: evaluation makes the claim, substantiation proves it.
questions.teaching:
Reviews do two different things, and the language of each is distinguishable.

Some wording simply reports: it states what happens, who is in it, how long it runs. Other wording expresses a judgement about how good, valuable or effective something is — words like compelling, clumsy, uneven, remarkable. That second kind is what carries the reviewer's opinion, and it is what analysis of a review should quote. Description on its own, however detailed, is not making a judgement, and that distinction is what the question tests.

questions.stem: A music reviewer writes: 'The band's second album is a wet blanket thrown over a very good party.' Beyond simply saying the album is disappointing, the metaphor adds the suggestion that the album:
options: was judged by a neutral critic who avoided taking any position
is being compared using the signal words 'like' or 'as'
smothers the energy and enjoyment the band had already created
was actually recorded during a party the band held together
questions.explanation: A metaphor works by carrying across the associations of the image: a wet blanket dampens something that was already alight, so the album is judged as killing momentum the band had built. The option about recording at a party reads the metaphor literally, which figurative language is never meant to be. Ask what the image is associated with, then apply those associations to the thing being judged.

questions.stem: A reviewer could call a fast-paced play 'a whirlwind' or 'a runaway car'. Choosing 'a runaway car' instead of 'a whirlwind' mainly:
options: tells the reader literally that a car appeared in the play
adds a sense of danger and lost control to the evaluation
converts the metaphor into a simile requiring 'like' or 'as'
removes the writer's opinion so the sentence becomes factual
questions.explanation: Different images carry different associations, and a runaway car brings ideas of hazard and something heading for a crash, so the judgement of the play shifts accordingly. The option claiming the sentence becomes factual is wrong because both images are figurative and both express a clear opinion. When comparing two metaphors, list what each image makes you feel, not just what it describes.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a simile to evaluate a film?
options: The final act lasts far too long and loses all tension.
The final act drags, bores and finally exhausts the viewer.
The final act crawls along like a queue at the supermarket.
The final act is a long, slow crawl towards nothing.
questions.explanation: A simile makes an explicit comparison between two unlike things using 'like' or 'as', and here the slow final act is compared to a supermarket queue, which carries the evaluation. The option calling the act 'a long, slow crawl towards nothing' is tempting because it is figurative, but it states the comparison directly without 'like' or 'as', so it is a metaphor, not a simile. The cue is the connecting word: 'like' or 'as' signals a simile, while a direct naming of one thing as another signals a metaphor.
questions.teaching:
Similes and metaphors both borrow qualities from one thing to describe another, and the difference is whether the comparison is announced.

A simile announces it, using 'like' or 'as'. A metaphor does not — it states the identity directly. So scanning the options for that linking word sorts them immediately. Note that the sentence also has to be doing evaluation, which means expressing a judgement about quality rather than simply describing what happens. Both conditions have to hold for the answer to be right.

questions.stem: In a review, 'substantiation' means the writer:
options: states an opinion about the text using strong, confident wording
summarises the plot of the text so readers know what happens
compares the text to another work by the same creator
backs up a judgement with evidence, examples or reasons from the text
questions.explanation: Substantiation is the support a writer gives for a claim — the evidence, detail or reasoning that makes the judgement convincing. 'States an opinion using strong, confident wording' is the closest trap, but that describes evaluation itself, which is the judgement being made, not the support for it. Remember the pair: evaluation is the verdict, substantiation is the proof offered for it.
questions.teaching:
An opinion in a review carries more weight when the reviewer shows why, and there is a term for that showing.

It means supporting a judgement with something concrete drawn from the work itself — a specific scene, a quoted line, an example of the technique being criticised. Without it, a review is a list of assertions the reader must take on trust. With it, the reader can check the reasoning and disagree on the evidence. This is the same demand made of any argument: the claim is one thing, the support for it is another.

questions.stem: A book reviewer writes: 'The novel's middle chapters are a swamp — every step forward sinks under another flashback.' The metaphor mainly strengthens the review by:
options: proving with quoted evidence that the flashbacks appear too often in the novel
softening the criticism so that readers see the novel as only mildly flawed
showing the reviewer's own writing skill rather than commenting on the book
turning a judgement about slowness into an image that also explains what causes it
questions.explanation: The swamp image carries the evaluation (the chapters are heavy going) and the second half of the sentence attaches a cause (repeated flashbacks), so the figurative language does evaluative and substantiating work at once. The option about proving with quoted evidence is tempting because the sentence names the flashbacks, but naming a feature in an image is not quoting or citing the text. Ask whether the words supply an image plus a reason, or an actual piece of textual evidence.

questions.stem: Two reviewers describe the same video game soundtrack. (i) 'The score is a heartbeat under every scene.' (ii) 'The score is wallpaper under every scene.' Compared with (i), the metaphor in (ii) evaluates the soundtrack as:
options: too loud and distracting, rather than well balanced with the dialogue
borrowed from another game, rather than composed for this one
ever-present but bland and easily ignored, rather than essential and alive
technically flawed and poorly recorded, rather than skilfully composed
questions.explanation: Both metaphors say the music is constantly there, but the associations differ: a heartbeat suggests life and necessity, while wallpaper suggests a background surface nobody notices, so (ii) judges the score as forgettable. 'Too loud and distracting' is the tempting misreading, but wallpaper carries the opposite connotation — it is unnoticed, not intrusive. When comparing metaphors, ask what qualities the source image is known for and transfer those to the thing being judged.

questions.stem: A set of instructions for assembling a flat-pack bookshelf is most likely structured as:
options: a thesis statement, several supporting arguments, then a restatement
a general classification, then paragraphs grouped by describing features
a goal, a list of materials or parts, then steps in time order
an orientation, a complication involving characters, then a resolution
questions.explanation: Structure follows purpose: the purpose of a procedure is to enable a reader to do something, so it states the goal, lists what is needed, and sequences the steps. The orientation–complication–resolution option is the structure of a narrative, whose purpose is to entertain through a problem and its outcome, which is not what instructions do. Thesis and arguments belong to persuasive exposition, and classification plus grouped description belongs to an information report. Name the purpose first, and the expected stages follow.

questions.stem: Which set of language features would you most expect in an information report about echidnas?
options: timeless present tense, general nouns such as 'echidnas', and technical vocabulary
past tense verbs, named individual animals as characters, and lines of dialogue
imperative verbs, numbered stages, and time connectives such as 'next' and 'then'
first-person opinions, high modality, and strongly emotive adjectives
questions.explanation: An information report classifies and describes a whole class of things, so it uses timeless present tense, generalised participants and field-specific technical terms. Past tense with named characters and dialogue belongs to a narrative or recount about one particular echidna, not to a report on the species. Imperatives with numbered stages signal a procedure, and first-person emotive opinion signals a persuasive text. The giveaway for a report is the general noun group: 'echidnas' rather than 'the echidna we saw'.

questions.stem: A news report begins: 'Three Year 8 students rescued a stranded penguin at Port Fairy yesterday.' Placing this sentence first reflects news report structure because:
options: news reports withhold the outcome until the final paragraph to build suspense
news reports must open with a thesis that the following paragraphs argue for
news reports begin with background context and save the main event for the end
the lead delivers the most newsworthy facts first, with less important detail following
questions.explanation: News reports are structured for readers who may stop reading at any point, so the lead answers who, what, where and when, and later paragraphs add quotations and background in decreasing importance. Delaying the outcome for suspense is a narrative technique, appropriate when the purpose is to entertain rather than to inform quickly. Opening with a thesis belongs to persuasive exposition. The cue is purpose: informing fast puts the key facts at the top.

questions.stem: A travel blog post retells the writer's day exploring Broome, then ends with a numbered list of tips for visiting the same places. This post is best described as a hybrid because it:
options: contains the writer's personal opinions, which convert any recount into a persuasive text
combines the time-ordered stages of a recount with the goal-and-steps work of a procedure
shifts between past and present tense, and any tense change makes a text a hybrid
is published online, and texts written for websites are automatically hybrid texts
questions.explanation: The post does two jobs at once: it recounts personal events in time order and it instructs readers on what to do, which is the structure and purpose of a procedure. Tense shifts on their own do not create a hybrid — plenty of single-purpose texts move between tenses within one structure. Nor does publishing online change a text's type, and including opinion does not by itself add a second set of stages. Look for two recognisable sets of stages doing two different jobs.

questions.stem: A student writes a research report on plastic waste for science, then adapts it into a speech for the school assembly. Which change best matches the shift in purpose and audience?
options: removing all statistics and evidence, because spoken texts cannot present numerical data
replacing the paragraphs with numbered steps, because speeches follow a procedure structure
delivering the identical wording, because content matters more than structure in any text
adding direct address and a clear call to action while keeping the key evidence and data
questions.explanation: The report's purpose is to inform an assessor, while the speech aims to inform and move a live audience to act, so the writer keeps the evidence but adds signposting, direct address to listeners and a call to action. Removing all statistics is wrong: spoken texts can and do use selected data, usually simplified and repeated for listeners. Speeches are not procedures, so numbered steps do not fit, and reusing identical wording ignores the fact that structure and language features change with purpose and audience.

questions.stem: Which sentence opener best signals that the evidence coming next CONTRASTS with the evidence just given?
options: For instance, the closing chapters give Ruth no dialogue at all.
In addition, the closing chapters give Ruth no dialogue at all.
In contrast, the closing chapters give Ruth no dialogue at all.
As a result, the closing chapters give Ruth no dialogue at all.
questions.explanation: Connectives signal the relationship between pieces of evidence: 'in contrast' marks opposition, 'as a result' marks cause and effect, 'for instance' introduces an example of a point already made, and 'in addition' adds a similar point. Students often reach for 'for instance' because it is the most common evidence signal, but an example supports the previous idea rather than opposing it. Cue: decide the relationship first, then choose the connective that names it.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'Jonas tells Asher the truth, but he refuses to listen.' Which revision most improves the cohesion of this sentence?
options: Delete 'but', so the two clauses are joined without an opposing connective.
Change the sentence to the passive voice: 'The truth is told to Asher.'
Add a quotation from the novel immediately after the word 'listen'.
Replace 'he' with 'Asher', so the reference word points clearly to one character.
questions.explanation: Cohesion depends on reference words that point unambiguously back to what they replace; here 'he' could mean Jonas or Asher, so naming Asher fixes the reference chain. Adding a quotation is tempting because evidence does strengthen paragraphs, but it does nothing about the unclear pronoun and the sentence would still confuse the reader. Cue: when a pronoun could refer to two people already mentioned, replace it with the noun.

questions.stem: A paragraph claims that the poet presents the drought as endless. Which continuation best SUBSTANTIATES that claim?
options: The poet grew up on a farm in northern Victoria during the 1990s, so the drought is described very convincingly in this poem.
The speaker describes 'another year of white sky', and the word 'another' turns one dry season into a repeating pattern with no end in sight.
The speaker describes 'another year of white sky', which is a striking and very memorable image in the second stanza of the poem.
The speaker's family have already sold most of their sheep, and then the neighbours leave the district for the coast in the final stanza.
questions.explanation: Substantiation means the quotation is followed by analysis that explains how the specific wording supports the claim — here, how 'another' creates a sense of endless repetition. Calling the image 'striking and memorable' quotes evidence but only praises it, so the link back to 'endless' is never made. Retelling what happens is plot summary, and biographical facts about the poet are not evidence from the text. Cue: after a quotation, ask 'how do these exact words prove my claim?'

questions.stem: 'Councils across Victoria have removed rubbish bins from several parks. ______ has cut litter by encouraging visitors to carry their waste home.' Which option fills the gap with a nominalisation that links the two sentences?
options: This removal
Because of this
They have removed
Removing bins they
questions.explanation: Nominalisation turns the verb 'removed' into the noun 'removal', so 'This removal' packages the whole previous sentence into a subject that the second sentence can comment on — a common academic cohesion device. 'Because of this' is tempting because it clearly refers back, but it is a prepositional phrase, not a noun, so it cannot be the subject of 'has cut' and the sentence becomes ungrammatical. Cue: the gap is followed by 'has cut', so it must be filled by a noun group.

questions.stem: Four students write about the claim 'the author builds tension through short sentences'. Whose sentence substantiates the claim most effectively?
options: The author uses many short sentences in this chapter, which clearly and obviously creates a great deal of tension.
The chapter opens with a long, flowing description of the coastline before the family arrive at the empty holiday house.
Three one-word sentences appear in a row — 'Nothing. Waiting. Again.' — and the full stops force pauses that stall the action.
The tension in this chapter is extremely intense, incredibly gripping and genuinely terrifying for the reader throughout.
questions.explanation: Effective substantiation names the specific feature, quotes it, and explains the effect of that feature — here the full stops that break the rhythm. Asserting that the writing 'clearly and obviously creates a great deal of tension' repeats the claim with intensifiers instead of proving it, which is the most tempting trap because it sounds confident. Piling up adjectives is emotive rather than analytical, and quoting long flowing description contradicts the claim about short sentences. Cue: strong evidence can be pointed to in the text; strong-sounding adverbs cannot.

questions.stem: In an analytical essay, the main job of the topic sentence at the start of a body paragraph is to:
options: present the strongest quotation from the text so the reader meets the evidence first
repeat the previous paragraph's evidence in different words so the reader remembers it
supply the page number and chapter of the evidence that the paragraph will use
state the claim the paragraph will prove and link it to the essay's overall argument
questions.explanation: Cohesion depends on internal structure: each paragraph opens with a claim that both signals what is coming and connects back to the thesis, so the reader can follow the sequence of the argument. Presenting the strongest quotation first is tempting, but a quotation is evidence, and evidence has no meaning until a claim tells the reader what it is supposed to prove. The cue is that a topic sentence should be in your own words and should be arguable, not quoted or referenced.

questions.stem: A student wants to use the words 'a stubborn, hopeful boy' from a novel as evidence. Which sentence embeds the quotation most effectively?
options: 'A stubborn, hopeful boy.' This quotation shows the reader what Kit is really like.
Kit is described as. 'A stubborn, hopeful boy' which hints he will not give up easily.
Kit is 'a stubborn, hopeful boy', he will not give up and this shows his character.
Kit is described as 'a stubborn, hopeful boy', a pairing that hints he will not give up.
questions.explanation: An embedded quotation must sit inside a grammatical sentence of your own and be followed by comment that links it to the claim. The version that drops the quotation in as its own fragment then adds a vague sentence is tempting because the punctuation looks tidy, but the quotation is not part of any clause and 'shows what Kit is really like' explains nothing. Check that your sentence still reads correctly as a sentence when the quotation marks are removed, and that a comma is not being used to join two complete statements.

questions.stem: A paragraph reads: 'The poet presents the city as exhausting. She writes that the streets are "a machine that never sleeps".' To complete the claim–evidence–explanation sequence, the next sentence should:
options: describe where the poet grew up and how long she lived in an inner-city suburb
state again that the poet clearly presents the city as an exhausting place to be
explain how the machine image makes the city seem relentless and draining for those in it
add a second quotation from a later stanza that also mentions streets and traffic
questions.explanation: Substantiation is only complete when the writer shows how the evidence proves the claim, so the sentence after a quotation should analyse its wording and tie it back to the argument. Adding a second quotation is the most tempting option, but stacking evidence without analysis leaves the reader to do the reasoning and weakens cohesion. The cue is that after a quotation the next sentence should contain words like 'suggests', 'implies' or 'makes the reader feel', not another set of quotation marks.

questions.stem: In grammar, a clause is best defined as:
options: any group of words that is separated from the rest of a sentence by commas
a complete sentence only, since a clause can never sit inside a larger sentence
a group of words built around a verb, which may be a main clause or a subordinate clause
a group of words that adds detail but contains no verb, such as 'in the old shed'
questions.explanation: A clause is a grammatical unit organised around a verb; main clauses can stand alone, while subordinate clauses depend on a main clause and are often embedded in it. The option describing a group of words with no verb defines a phrase, not a clause, which is the most common mix-up. The quick test is to look for a verb: no verb means phrase, verb means clause.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains an embedded relative clause?
options: After waiting all week, the students boarded the late bus.
The late bus arrived at the stop beside the school oval.
The bus, which had been late all week, finally arrived on time.
The bus was late all week, so nobody expected it on time.
questions.explanation: 'which had been late all week' has its own verb and sits inside the main clause, adding information about the noun 'bus' — that is an embedded relative clause. The sentence joined by 'so' is tempting, but it links two main clauses side by side rather than embedding one inside the other. Look for a relative pronoun such as who, which or that introducing extra detail about a noun.
questions.teaching:
A relative clause adds information about a noun, and an embedded one sits inside the sentence rather than at the end.

It usually begins with who, which, that, whose or where, and it interrupts the main sentence to describe the noun just before it. When the information is extra rather than essential, it is fenced off with commas — lift the whole thing out and the sentence still works. Spotting one means finding the relative pronoun and checking whether what follows describes the noun immediately preceding it.

questions.stem: 'Although the storm had passed, the netball courts were still flooded.' The main clause is:
options: the storm had passed
Although the storm had passed, the netball courts
the netball courts were still flooded
Although the storm had passed
questions.explanation: The main clause makes sense on its own and carries the central idea; 'the netball courts were still flooded' does both. 'Although the storm had passed' is tempting because it comes first, but the subordinating conjunction 'although' makes it dependent. Removing the conjunction ('the storm had passed') does not make it the main clause of this sentence — it is still the subordinate clause with its marker stripped off.
questions.teaching:
A complex sentence has one clause that could stand alone and one that could not, and telling them apart is the whole task.

The dependent clause usually opens with a subordinating conjunction — although, because, when, while, if, since. That opening word is what makes it unable to stand on its own: read it aloud by itself and you are left waiting. Strip that clause away and what remains is a complete sentence, and that remainder is the main one. So find the subordinating word first, and everything it introduces is the part that depends.

questions.stem: Which sentence places an embedded clause between the subject and its verb?
options: Because she submitted early, Mia won first prize for her essay.
Mia submitted her essay last night, and it won first prize.
The essay that Mia submitted last night won first prize.
Mia submitted the essay that won first prize last night.
questions.explanation: In the correct sentence, the subject is 'The essay' and its verb is 'won', with the relative clause 'that Mia submitted last night' tucked in between them — the classic embedded position. The sentence with 'the essay that won first prize' also has a relative clause, but it comes after the object at the end of the sentence, not inside the subject–verb link. Test it by finding the subject and its verb, then checking whether a clause interrupts them.

questions.stem: 'Volunteers replanted the creek bank ______' Which addition expands the sentence with a clause that gives a reason?
options: after heavy rain in the middle of June
for the sake of the local platypus population
during the last week of the winter holidays
because erosion had washed away the topsoil
questions.explanation: 'because erosion had washed away the topsoil' contains its own verb ('had washed') and the conjunction 'because' signals cause, so it is a subordinate clause adding a reason. 'for the sake of the local platypus population' is tempting because it hints at purpose, but it has no verb, so it is a phrase, not a clause. Check for a verb first, then check what the linking word signals: reason, time, condition or contrast.

questions.stem: Which sentence punctuates its embedded clause correctly?
options: My uncle who lives in Ballarat, is driving down on Sunday.
My uncle, who lives in Ballarat is driving down on Sunday.
My uncle who, lives in Ballarat, is driving down on Sunday.
My uncle, who lives in Ballarat, is driving down on Sunday.
questions.explanation: When an embedded clause adds extra, non-essential information, it needs a comma at both ends so the main clause reads smoothly once the clause is lifted out. The version with a single comma before 'is' is the most tempting, but it closes an interruption that was never opened, leaving the subject cut off from its verb. Read the sentence without the clause: if it still works, the clause needs a matching pair of commas.

questions.stem: Three sentences: 'The mural covers the gym wall.' 'Students painted it in Term 2.' 'It shows local wildlife.' Which version combines them using an embedded relative clause?
options: Painted in Term 2 by students, the mural on the gym wall shows local wildlife.
The mural, which students painted in Term 2, covers the gym wall and shows local wildlife.
Students painted the mural in Term 2, and it covers the gym wall, and it shows local wildlife.
The mural covers the gym wall, showing local wildlife, painted by students in Term 2.
questions.explanation: 'which students painted in Term 2' has its own subject and verb and is embedded inside the main clause between the subject and its verbs, so it is a relative clause doing the combining work. The version beginning 'Painted in Term 2 by students' is tempting because it also front-loads that detail, but 'Painted in Term 2 by students' is a participle phrase with no subject and no finite verb. Check for a relative pronoun plus a subject and verb before calling something an embedded clause.

questions.stem: 'The bus that stops outside the aquatic centre runs every twenty minutes.' What does the embedded clause 'that stops outside the aquatic centre' do in this sentence?
options: It states the main action that the whole sentence is reporting
It works as the subject that the verb 'runs' agrees with
It joins two complete independent clauses with a conjunction
It adds information identifying which bus the writer means
questions.explanation: An embedded relative clause sits inside the noun group and adds detail about the noun, here narrowing 'the bus' down to one particular service. The option calling it the main action is tempting because the clause contains the verb 'stops', but the main action of the sentence is 'runs every twenty minutes' — the embedded clause is only a modifier of the noun. A useful cue: read the sentence with the clause removed; if what remains ('The bus runs every twenty minutes') is still a complete sentence, the clause was embedded extra information, not the main clause, subject or a second independent clause.

questions.stem: Nominalisation is best defined as:
options: replacing a noun with a pronoun so that the same noun is not repeated across sentences
adding a suffix such as -ly to an adjective so it can describe how an action is done
changing a verb or adjective into a noun, so an action or quality is expressed as a thing
changing a noun into a verb, so a thing is expressed as an action the reader can picture
questions.explanation: Nominalisation compresses a process or quality into a noun: 'decide' becomes 'decision', 'reliable' becomes 'reliability'. The option describing a noun turning into a verb reverses the direction of the change — that is verbalisation, and it makes writing more active, not more abstract. The cue is the ending: nominalisations usually end in -tion, -ment, -ity, -ance or -ness.

questions.stem: Which pair shows a verb changed into a nominalisation?
options: happy → happily
investigate → investigation
beauty → beautiful
quick → quicker
questions.explanation: 'Investigate' is a verb naming an action, and 'investigation' turns that action into a noun — the defining move of nominalisation. 'Beauty → beautiful' is tempting because a suffix is added, but it goes the wrong way: a noun becomes an adjective. Check that the starting word names an action or quality and the finished word names a thing.
questions.teaching:
Formal writing often turns actions into things, and the process has a name.

A verb describing something happening becomes a noun naming the happening: 'decide' becomes 'decision', 'investigate' becomes something you can put an article in front of. Adjectives do it too — 'happy' becomes 'happiness'. The effect is to pack more into a sentence and sound authoritative, which is why reports and academic writing are full of it. The cost is that the actor disappears, so it is always worth asking who actually did the thing.

questions.stem: In which text would you expect the highest density of nominalisation?
options: A conversation between two students about last night's football match
A picture book written for children in their first year of school
A government report analysing household water use across Victoria
A quick text message to a friend arranging to meet at the station
questions.explanation: Nominalisation suits formal, information-dense writing such as reports, because abstract nouns like 'consumption', 'restriction' and 'reduction' pack a lot of meaning into few words and sound objective. Casual conversation is the most tempting alternative for students who think nominalisation just means 'long words', but speech relies on verbs and named participants so listeners can follow it in real time. Ask whether the text needs density and distance, or immediacy.

questions.stem: 'Scientists observed the reef for ten years.' Which continuation carries the idea forward using a nominalisation?
options: What the scientists saw was a steady decline in coral cover.
These observations showed a steady decline in coral cover.
They observed a steady decline in coral cover over that time.
Observing carefully, they watched the coral cover decline.
questions.explanation: 'Observations' turns the action of the first sentence into a noun that can then act as the subject of the next sentence — a common way nominalisation builds cohesion in reports. 'Observing carefully' is tempting because it looks noun-like, but it works here as a participle phrase describing how the scientists watched, not as a noun naming the process. Check whether the word can take 'these' or 'the' in front of it and act as a subject.

questions.stem: Compare: (i) 'Students damaged the bike shed overnight.' (ii) 'Damage to the bike shed occurred overnight.' The main effect of the nominalised version (ii) is that it:
options: supplies a time reference that the first version does not give the reader
presents the event as a thing that happened, leaving out who was responsible
names those responsible more precisely while adding emotional weight to the event
turns the noun 'damage' into a verb, making the sentence sound more active
questions.explanation: Nominalising 'damaged' into the noun 'damage' removes the need for a doer, so the reader is told what occurred but not who did it — which is why officials and report writers often choose this wording. The option about naming those responsible reverses the effect: version (i) is the one that names the students. Both sentences contain 'overnight', so the time reference is unchanged.

questions.stem: For a school assembly speech, a student drafts: 'The implementation of a reduction in the utilisation of plastic bottles is a recommendation of this report.' The main problem with this sentence for a listening audience is that:
options: it contains no nouns at all, so listeners are given nothing concrete
too many pronouns are used, so listeners lose track of who is speaking
it lacks a main verb, so it is a fragment rather than a full sentence
stacked abstract nouns make it dense and leave unclear who must act
questions.explanation: 'Implementation', 'reduction', 'utilisation' and 'recommendation' are all nominalisations, so processes pile up as things and no participant is named — hard work for a listener who cannot reread. Saying it lacks a main verb is tempting because the actions have disappeared into nouns, but 'is' is the main verb and the sentence is grammatically complete. The giveaway of over-nominalisation is a string of -tion nouns with only a weak linking verb between them.

questions.stem: Which rewrite of 'The implementation of a reduction in the utilisation of plastic bottles is a recommendation of this report.' best undoes the nominalisation for a spoken audience?
options: The recommendation of this report is a reduction in plastic bottle use.
A reduction in the use of plastic bottles is recommended by this report.
Plastic bottle usage reduction is the central recommendation of this report.
We recommend that the school use far fewer plastic bottles this year.
questions.explanation: Undoing nominalisation means turning the abstract nouns back into verbs and naming the participants: 'recommend' and 'use' become verbs, and 'we' and 'the school' appear as doers. The version beginning 'A reduction in the use...' is tempting because it sounds tidier, but 'reduction' and 'use' remain nouns and the passive 'is recommended' still hides the people involved. Check each option for a real action verb with a named doer in front of it.

questions.stem: A council report states: 'The rejection of the proposal followed lengthy consultation with residents.' Which effect of nominalisation is at work in this sentence?
options: Actions have been packaged as nouns, so the report reads as formal and the people who rejected and consulted are not named
Actions have been packaged as nouns, which makes the sentence longer but leaves the doers of the actions clearly named
Verbs have been added to the sentence, so the events sound more immediate and the residents seem more powerful
Adjectives have replaced the verbs, so the sentence records the writer's opinion of the proposal rather than an event
questions.explanation: Nominalisation turns processes into noun groups — here 'reject' becomes 'the rejection' and 'consult' becomes 'consultation' — which compresses information, raises the formality, and lets the writer leave out who actually did the rejecting. The option claiming the doers are still clearly named is tempting because 'residents' appears, but residents are only who was consulted; nobody is identified as rejecting the proposal. The cue: look for nouns ending in -ion, -ment or -ance where you would expect a verb, then ask 'who did this?' — if you can't tell, the nominalisation has hidden the agent.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?
options: We packed three things; sunscreen, hats and water.
The tram was cancelled; and we walked to the station instead.
The tram was cancelled; we walked to the station instead.
Because the tram was cancelled; we walked to the station instead.
questions.explanation: A semicolon must have a complete, independent clause on each side, and 'The tram was cancelled' and 'we walked to the station instead' both qualify. The most tempting error is 'We packed three things; sunscreen, hats and water', but a list introduced by a complete clause takes a colon, since the list itself is not an independent clause. Also remember that a semicolon replaces a joining word like 'and', so it should not be used in front of one.
questions.teaching:
A semicolon links two statements that could each have stood alone as sentences, when they are closely enough related that a full stop would break the thought.

So the test has two parts. First, check that what sits either side of the mark is a complete statement with its own subject and verb. Second, check the two are genuinely connected in meaning. If one side is a fragment, the mark is wrong and a comma or a dash is wanted instead. Using it to introduce a list is the other common error — that belongs to the colon.

questions.stem: What does a PAIR of dashes do in a sentence such as 'The captain — usually the calmest player on the court — snapped at the umpire'?
options: It separates items in a list that already contains commas inside the items
It marks the point where a subordinate clause is joined to the main clause
It shows that the writer is quoting someone else's exact words
It inserts extra, non-essential information into the sentence with added emphasis
questions.explanation: Paired dashes act like strong brackets: the sentence still reads correctly if the dashed material is removed, and the dashes give that inserted comment extra punch. 'It separates items in a list that already contains commas' describes semicolons, which are used to keep complicated lists clear. The cue for paired dashes is that you can lift out the words between them and the sentence still stands.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses semicolons correctly to keep a complicated list clear?
options: The exchange students came from Osaka, Japan, Busan, South Korea; and Hanoi, Vietnam.
The exchange students came from Osaka, Japan; Busan, South Korea; and Hanoi, Vietnam.
The exchange students came from Osaka; Japan, Busan; South Korea, and Hanoi; Vietnam.
The exchange students came from; Osaka, Japan, Busan, South Korea, and Hanoi, Vietnam.
questions.explanation: When the items in a list already contain commas, semicolons mark the boundaries between whole items so the reader can see where each one ends. The version that separates city from country with a semicolon reverses the logic: the semicolon must divide the items, not the parts inside an item. A semicolon also never introduces a list, so it cannot follow 'came from'.

questions.stem: 'By the end of the working bee there was one job left — repainting the goalposts.' What is the dash doing here?
options: Signalling that the writer has interrupted a direct quotation from a speaker
Separating two items in a list so the reader does not confuse them
Adding an abrupt, emphasised detail that completes the idea in the opening clause
Joining two independent clauses that could each stand alone as a sentence
questions.explanation: A single dash builds a pause and then delivers information with emphasis; here 'repainting the goalposts' names the job and lands with a small dramatic effect. 'Joining two independent clauses' is tempting because dashes can sometimes do that, but 'repainting the goalposts' has no subject and verb of its own, so it is not an independent clause. Check what sits after the dash: a phrase means the dash is adding emphasis, not joining sentences.

questions.stem: Compare: (i) 'My cousin, who had never surfed before, stood up on her first wave.' (ii) 'My cousin — who had never surfed before — stood up on her first wave.' What does the change to dashes mainly do?
options: It turns the interrupting words into a clause that could stand alone as a sentence
It shows that the interrupting words have been added by an editor, not the writer
It gives the interrupting information a sharper break and stronger emphasis than commas do
It signals that the information is now essential for identifying which cousin is meant
questions.explanation: Dashes are a louder version of paired commas: the extra information is still non-essential, but the reader feels a stronger interruption and notices the detail more. The claim that the information becomes 'essential for identifying which cousin' is wrong — dashes, like commas, mark the relative clause as non-defining; essential clauses take no surrounding punctuation at all. Judge emphasis by the strength of the mark, and defining versus non-defining by whether any punctuation is there in the first place.

questions.stem: 'The forecast promised sunshine, the carnival was rained out by midday.' Which revision fixes the punctuation error?
options: The forecast promised sunshine, however, the carnival was rained out by midday.
Although the forecast promised sunshine; the carnival was rained out by midday.
The forecast promised sunshine; but the carnival was rained out by midday.
The forecast promised sunshine; the carnival was rained out by midday.
questions.explanation: The original is a comma splice: two independent clauses joined by nothing but a comma, which a semicolon can correctly repair. The version with 'however' between commas is the most tempting fix, but 'however' is not a coordinating conjunction, so it cannot hold two independent clauses together with commas — that is still a splice. The cue: only 'and, but, or, so, yet, for, nor' can join clauses after a comma; words like 'however' need a semicolon or full stop in front of them.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly with the connecting word 'however'?
options: The tickets sold out in an hour, however; extra seats were released on Friday.
The tickets sold out in an hour, however, extra seats were released on Friday.
The tickets sold out in an hour; however extra seats, were released on Friday.
The tickets sold out in an hour; however, extra seats were released on Friday.
questions.explanation: A semicolon joins two clauses that could each stand alone, and when a connective such as 'however' introduces the second clause, the semicolon goes before it and a comma follows it. Placing the semicolon after 'however' is the most tempting error, but it cuts 'however' away from the clause it introduces and leaves only a comma joining the two main clauses. Using commas on both sides of 'however' creates a comma splice, because a comma is too weak to join two complete sentences. The cue: the semicolon marks the join between the two clauses, so it sits before the connective, never after it.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'The museum's new wing opened in March; attracting record crowds every weekend since.' Why is the semicolon incorrect here?
options: A semicolon must always be followed by a connective such as 'however' or 'therefore'
The two ideas are unrelated, so the semicolon should be replaced with a full stop
What follows the semicolon is a phrase, not a clause that could stand alone as a sentence
Semicolons can only separate items in a long list, never join two parts of a sentence
questions.explanation: A semicolon joins two independent clauses — each side must be able to stand alone as a sentence. Here 'attracting record crowds every weekend since' has no subject and finite verb of its own, so a comma is the right mark. The suggestion that a semicolon needs a connective like 'however' is tempting because that pattern is common, but a semicolon works perfectly well without one when both sides are complete clauses. The cue: cover the semicolon and test whether each side reads as a full sentence on its own.

questions.stem: What is the subject of "The old dog barked loudly"?
options: Loudly
Dog barked
The old dog
Barked
questions.explanation: The subject is who or what performs the verb, including the words describing it. Barked is the verb and loudly modifies it.

questions.stem: Which sentence is in the passive voice?
options: Breaking windows is dangerous
The window was broken by the storm
The storm broke the window
The storm was strong
questions.explanation: In the passive the thing acted on comes first and the doer moves to the end or disappears. The active version names the storm as the subject.

questions.stem: Why might a writer choose the passive voice?
options: To show the action happened twice
To turn a statement into a question
To keep the focus off who did it
To make the sentence shorter
questions.explanation: The passive lets the doer be left out entirely, which is why official writing uses it so often. That can be useful or evasive depending on the intent.

questions.stem: What is a clause?
options: A group of words with its own verb
Any group of words in a sentence
A group of words in brackets
A sentence with no punctuation
questions.explanation: Every clause has a verb, which is what separates it from a phrase. A sentence can hold one clause or several.

questions.stem: Which is a subordinate clause?
options: Rain, wind and hail
Although it was raining
It was raining heavily
The rain fell
questions.explanation: A subordinate clause cannot stand alone as a sentence, and the word although is what makes it dependent. The others are complete or have no verb.

questions.stem: Which sentence is a compound sentence?
options: She read the book and he watched the film
She read the book quietly
Reading the book, she smiled
Because she read the book
questions.explanation: A compound sentence joins two independent clauses with a conjunction. Each half could stand alone as its own sentence.

questions.stem: Where does the comma go in "After the storm passed we went outside"?
options: After "storm"
After "we"
No comma is needed
After "passed"
questions.explanation: A subordinate clause at the start of a sentence is followed by a comma. If it came second, the comma would usually be dropped.

questions.stem: Why is "The bus was late; we missed the film" correctly punctuated?
options: A conjunction has been left out on purpose
The first half is longer than the second half
Both halves are complete sentences and closely related
The second half explains a word in the first half
questions.explanation: A semicolon joins two complete, closely related sentences without a conjunction. If either half could not stand alone, a comma or a colon would be needed instead.

questions.stem: What does a colon do in "She had one rule: never look back"?
options: Introduces an explanation of what came before
Joins two unrelated ideas
Marks a pause for breath
Shows that words are missing
questions.explanation: A colon points forward to what follows, which explains or lists what the first part promised. A semicolon would simply link two equal halves.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a dangling modifier?
options: Running for the bus, she was soaked
She was soaked while running for the bus
The rain soaked her as she ran
Running for the bus, the rain soaked her
questions.explanation: The opening phrase should describe the subject that follows, but here it attaches to the rain, which cannot run. Rearranging fixes it.

questions.stem: What is the tense of "She had finished before he arrived"?
options: Past perfect
Simple past
Present perfect
Future perfect
questions.explanation: The past perfect shows one past action completed before another. It is what makes the order of two past events clear.

questions.stem: Which pronoun correctly completes "Between you and ___"?
options: myself
mine
me
I
questions.explanation: After a preposition the object form is needed, so it is me. The temptation to use I comes from a mistaken sense that it sounds more correct.

questions.stem: Which sentence has correct subject-verb agreement?
options: The lists of item is on the table
The list of item are on the table
The list of items is on the table
The list of items are on the table
questions.explanation: The subject is list, which is singular, so the verb is singular too. The plural noun between them is what misleads.

questions.stem: What is the function of "however" in a sentence?
options: It states the result that follows from the point
It signals a contrast with what came before
It adds a further point supporting the same idea
It introduces an example of the point just made
questions.explanation: Connectives signpost the relationship between ideas, and however marks a turn. Using the wrong connective misleads the reader about the argument.

questions.stem: Which is the correct punctuation for speech?
options: "Wait." she said. "I have an idea."
"Wait", she said "I have an idea".
Wait, she said, I have an idea.
"Wait," she said, "I have an idea."
questions.explanation: Commas sit inside the quotation marks and the speech tag is enclosed by them. Full stops only end the speech when the sentence ends.

questions.stem: What is an adverbial phrase?
options: A group of words in brackets
A group of words telling how, when or where
A group of words naming a person or thing
A group of words with no verb
questions.explanation: Adverbials answer the same questions single adverbs do, but across several words. In the morning and with great care are both adverbial.

questions.stem: Why would a writer use a very short paragraph?
options: To save space on the page
To show a change of speaker
To indicate a quotation follows
To give a single idea emphasis
questions.explanation: Isolating a sentence in its own paragraph makes the reader slow down on it. Paragraph length is as deliberate as sentence length.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a relative clause?
options: The book that she borrowed was overdue
She borrowed the book yesterday
The overdue book was hers
She borrowed it and returned it
questions.explanation: A relative clause begins with who, which or that and adds information about a noun. Here it tells us which book is meant.

questions.stem: What is the imperative mood used for?
options: Asking questions
Describing the past
Expressing doubt
Giving commands or instructions
questions.explanation: Imperatives drop the subject and start with the verb, as in "Close the door". Recipes and instruction manuals are written almost entirely in them.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains a rhetorical question?
options: Where did you put the keys?
Which bus goes to town?
Who wouldn't want a safer school?
What time does school start?
questions.explanation: A rhetorical question expects no answer, because the answer is assumed. It is a persuasive device rather than a genuine request.

questions.stem: What does an ellipsis usually signal?
options: A list continuing
Words left out or a trailing pause
A sudden interruption
A change of speaker
questions.explanation: Three dots mark omitted words in a quotation or a sentence trailing away. A dash marks an abrupt break instead.

questions.stem: Which revision makes "The reason is because it rained" correct?
options: The reason is because of rain
The reason why is because it rained
It rained is the reason because
The reason is that it rained
questions.explanation: Reason and because both express cause, so using them together repeats the idea. Replacing because with that removes the redundancy.
